slot.brief: Unsymmetrical ether (aryl–alkyl type) treated with excess HI; ask the organic products and why the aryl–O bond does not cleave — SN2 vs SN1 reasoning at harder level.

stem: Ethoxybenzene is heated with excess HI. Which choice gives the organic products and correctly explains why the aryl–O bond remains intact?
options: Iodobenzene and ethanol; iodide displaces at the aryl carbon by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$.
Iodobenzene and ethanol; aryl–O cleavage occurs by formation of a phenyl cation.
Iodoethane and phenol; iodide attacks the ethyl carbon by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, while the aryl C–O bond is not cleaved.
Iodoethane and iodobenzene; excess HI replaces the phenolic –OH by iodine.

verdicts.working: HI protonates the ether; I⁻ attacks the ethyl carbon by S_N2, giving iodoethane and phenol. The aryl C–O bond is not cleaved because the aryl carbon does not undergo S_N2 substitution.

working:
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5+\text{HI}\to\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}+\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I}$. Iodide attacks the primary ethyl carbon by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$; the aryl C(sp$^2$)–O bond resists $\text{S}_\text{N}2$, and a phenyl cation is highly unstable.

Independent check: HI protonates the ether; I⁻ attacks the ethyl carbon by S_N2, giving iodoethane and phenol. The aryl C–O bond is not cleaved because the aryl carbon does not undergo S_N2 substitution.
solution:
HI protonates the ether oxygen; iodide then attacks the primary ethyl carbon by $\text{S}_\text{N}2$.
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OC}_2\text{H}_5+\text{HI}\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}+\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{I}$$
The aryl C(sp$^2$)–O bond remains intact because aryl carbon does not undergo $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ substitution; a phenyl cation is also highly unstable.
